D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Ming Gives Way to Wu
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Ming–Wu Succession: Zheng Zhao’s Audience

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
In spring 1678, Zheng Zhao - Duke of Wu in Northern Ming, Nanjing regent and minister of rites - after a chain of military victories at home and abroad, petitioned the court to enter the capital and pay homage to the Ming Son of Heaven. At that time, the Tianjin Prince of Yan, victor of the great constitutional war thirty years earlier, still blazed in power. Yet Zheng's stubbornness overcame counsel and threats alike, and the journey took place that June.

This audience became a grand procession unseen for nearly three centuries, from warlord age to feudal-prince age in Northern Ming. Though coerced by Yan, Qin, and Qi powers into bringing only 5,000 guards and officials, Zheng's train contained elite land-sea forces of Wu's era: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese shield-swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadier units, even an exiled noble group of 'Far Eastern Yin people' seeking troops from the Chinese emperor. It carried treasures won by Wu over a century of global campaigns, plus Annamese and Khmer tribute rice borne by nearly ten thousand laborers. In stark contrast stood the famine-struck Central Plains under transport extortion and local armed strife.

After returning, Zheng Zhao at once took the title 'Supreme One.' Wu then entered rapid growth as refugees from north and south poured into its core and colonies. Zheng and his successors pushed harsh centralizing 'autocratic reform' and land commodification, ultimately securing our foundation as Southern Court overlord directing all nations. Wu's march has never ceased - to this very day...
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

The founding emperor rose from beggary, destroyed foreign rule and restored the Chinese heartland. His achievements would outlast the inscriptions of history. Though virtue might decline, the mandate seemed unchanged. Yet today I have seen him: the Zhu boy is mortal too.\n—Zheng Zhao

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: After the Chief Minister’s Death

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
Chen Dongyang (courtesy name Manyue, 1772-[Date.GetString|v]) was a leading civic republican thinker and founding hero of the short-lived Western Qin revolutionary republic. Exiled from his own state, he worked with southern progressives and became chief architect of Southern Ming modernization as chief minister.

Yet reform brought fierce political upheaval and resistance from local power holders. As reform reached completion, Zheng Qin and allies came to fear republican ideals beyond their control. On [Date.GetString|v], while Chen departed for lecture tours in the Far East Continent, an unidentified Wa ronin shot him dead on deck with a short firearm.

After Chen's death, southern republicans who followed him immediately fell into accusation and factional dispute. Deng Mingyu, minister of revenue and fellow 'Four Gentlemen of the Republic,' moved toward Zheng Qin and the Southern Office. Zheng Diaojin, former administrator of Huguang, led part of the faction west to Sichuan under Xiao Huli.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Chen Dongyang is dead. Southern republicans have lost the leader of their reforms, while the cabinet and Six Ministries must redistribute his responsibilities. Provincial delegates still debate reform’s future in the Assembly of Rites, but Hangzhou is already courting the officials left without their leader.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Zhu of Ming, or Zheng of Wu? For politically active citizens of the Southern Court, this is a question asked every minute. From lecture platforms in Sichuan border schools to debate halls in Nanjing's ministry of rites, arguments, memorials, essays, and reports cry out everywhere. Yet there are more questions than answers, and more contention than deliberation.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Ming’s Zhu dynasty, or Wu’s Zheng house? For those able to take part in Southern Chinese politics, the question demands an answer at every moment. From village lecture halls on Sichuan’s frontier to the chamber of the Ministry of Rites in Nanjing, arguments, memorials, essays and reports call out to the public. There are more questions than answers, more quarrels than considered debate.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: About two centuries ago, the Toyotomi shogunate pacified Japan's Warring States with support from Wu's Prince of Ming, and later jointly defeated Korean forces backed by Yanjing Ming court and old Qi feudatory interests in struggles over Korea.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng foothold in Kyushu forms part of Wu’s maritime power and has long affected the interests of Japan’s great houses. With civil war threatening the Southern realm, rival envoys cross the sea seeking ships and supplies. The government has an opportunity to recover the Wu-held lands of Kyushu and reshape relations across the strait.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Zhu Banbo dead in battle, Chen Dongyang assassinated, Deng Mingyu defected, Zheng Diaojin fled west. Even mighty Mu Zhongtang, constrained by northern strife, cannot look south. In the Jinling palace no one remains who can face the Zheng-Wu Supreme directly. By China's millennia of history, dynastic transfer was only a matter of time - yet conservatives and reformers alike believed our age had transcended history. Dreams, however, seldom survive reality.\n\nAt that moment, by coincidence of Wu ruler's birthday, all Nanjing officials went to Hangzhou to offer congratulations, regardless of origin. In the Ming Gongzong court at Nanjing, only Zhu Jiangchen, son of old marshal Zhu Banbo and vice minister of war, remained. Three days later, Wu chancellor Hao Tingjiang and ten Wu ministers entered Jinling palace. Next day Gongzong enacted Yao-Shun style abdication in favor of Wu. Zheng Ju took the throne as emperor, proclaimed Great Wu, granted amnesty, and changed era to Tianyan, remembered as Emperor Tianyan and Wu Taizong. Ming Gongzong Zhu Kuobin was reduced to Ming feudatory prince and moved to Chongming Island in Fujian. A month later he was charged for excessive drinking at banquets; terrified, he hired a civilian vessel and fled eastward.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng family has demanded a new dynasty and recognition from the provinces and overseas states. Recognition accepts Zheng government under the new constitution; taking up arms for Ming requires allies and preparations against Hangzhou’s forces. Others would use the crisis to leave the existing hierarchy and govern independently.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
The Southern Ming turmoil that began with Wu-Ming dynastic transfer reached an unprecedented peak on [Date.GetString|v].

Former Ming loyalists, landlords sacrificed in land reform, and remnants of the early-century civic revolution - three groups with very different aims - united under pressure from the Zheng house of Southern Office. Zhu Jiangchen and Feng Yunshan of Chu, Wei Jian and Xiao Huli of Shu, Zhu Jingyin and Yang Xiuqing of Huai raised arms under the banner 'Overthrow Wu, restore Ming, pacify national calamity by Heaven's mandate.' Emperor Tianyan sent Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang, Lin Zexu, and Wu (Ii) Naosuke to suppress them.

When Tianyan took the throne, Southern Ming was nominally the world's leading empire. This upheaval shocked the world at once; from Far East Continent to distant England, states sent envoys. Today those envoys will witness a fierce eastern conflagration rekindled less than half a century after peace.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Proclamations against the succession have spread. Wu is assembling the central army to enforce recognition of Zheng rule; Ming loyalist provinces are gathering troops and supplies for common resistance. The Southern and Western Administrations, once united against the North, now face one another in arms.\n\nMaritime and river trade routes will carry armies and suffer the disruption of war. Overseas dependencies, neighbouring states and distant merchants must choose their course anew. Whoever wins will inherit the demands of those who shed blood for victory.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
Rather than full explosion of contradictions, decisive Southern Court politicians delayed imperial collapse through firm choices. Even amid Wu-Ming dynastic upheaval, regional governors chose no effective resistance and accepted Wu narratives of total corruption by the Ming emperor and his magnates, preserving a fragile peace in South China.

In one sense, this implies the sun-and-moon dynasty had long become rotten wood no one wished to die with. Zhu Kuobin, the last emperor to defend court order, may simply have been born at the wrong time.

Yet this survivor of four centuries of warlord politics lost much. The age of war-peace confrontation ended, but opponents, regional prejudice among old feudatory populations, and new radical groups still move in the shadows of the new era, cloaking the nation's road forward in dense fog.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Local opposition has failed to form a coalition for common war. Provinces and overseas states that remain loyal recognise Zheng rule, while others have left the previous hierarchy. Hangzhou can continue governing the centre, but cannot treat every silence as consent.\n\nThe new dynasty must appoint officials and govern under its constitution, while sustaining authority with the troops and revenues it possesses. Unresolved relations with the provinces and states will be shaped by future development, negotiation and conflict.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The internal chaos raised by Zheng traitors has finally ended in the victory of those on the righteous path. This is not an age to praise. Loyalists killed loyalists; republicans attacked republicans. Zheng's group was not originally the most rotten faction of old Ming, yet their thirst for power and singular status in the old state pushed all of us into the abyss of war. As victors, we must ensure this never repeats.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The coalition has defeated Wu’s central army. The Ming cause brought the Western provinces and their allies together; victory now raises another question: who will govern from Nanjing?\n\nThe Zhu house still claims the throne, while victorious provincial leaders are reluctant to surrender their military and political authority. Republicans want the citizens who fought together to share in a new deliberative government. Whether the wartime coalition can accommodate these demands will determine the Southern realm’s future constitution.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Zheng house and Japan's rulers are old acquaintances. Frankly, though they already became masters of China, in Tang-land precedent it is hardly unprecedented for masters to seek more; Zheng restraint has perhaps lasted too long. Yet Zheng-Wu elites have grown overconfident. In the shadows, opponents gather. This is a once-in-a-century opening. If civil war erupts in Ming (Wu), Japan - the largest outer feudatory of the Ming court - must quickly prepare to defend our interests and perhaps the order of Shenzhou itself.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Southern civil war has brought Kyushu back to the centre of Japanese politics. Zheng ports, trade routes and garrisons on the island support Wu’s maritime power and affect the interests of Japanese lords and merchants.\n\nBoth Wu and its opponents seek Japanese intervention, offering to return the Zheng-held parts of Kyushu after victory. The side we support will determine our allies across the sea and the government from which we must claim our reward.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 朱班博整顿湖广时曾修复襄阳工事，召集青年军官任教，又用军工铁件向川蜀换取粮食。伤兵与退伍军人分入后勤、屯垦卫所，留在襄阳的共和派协助总督府改造岳麓书院。二十年间，总督府的军队、田赋、学政渐成一体。加上朝廷中有陈东阳为奥援。时人多以襄阳兵为“新西府”的魁首。更是南明联邦建国不可或缺的柱石。\n\n然而，曾经极力支持朱斑博的郑家屡屡在朝廷中指责襄阳方面拖欠税款、瞒报户籍。又外放石元辅、林汉涵等亲湖广派的南兵高层和许多亲近湖广的共和派官员。一系列迹象表明我们必须做好最坏准备。重新核定屯田兵农丁口，接续上游的粮运，在书院中造势拉拢士子。以备不时之需。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: When Zhu Banbo reorganised Huguang, he repaired the fortifications of Xiangyang, brought young officers into teaching, and exchanged military ironware for grain from Sichuan. Wounded and retired soldiers entered supply services and farming garrisons. Republicans who remained in Xiangyang helped the governor-general reform Yuelu Academy. Over twenty years, the army, land revenues and academies became closely bound to his government, with Chen Dongyang supporting it at court. Xiangyang’s troops came to be regarded as the leaders of the New Western Administration, an indispensable pillar of the Southern Ming federation.\n\nThe Zheng family once supported Zhu Banbo vigorously. Now it repeatedly accuses Xiangyang of withholding taxes and concealing households. Southern officers friendly to Huguang, including Shi Yuanfu and Lin Hanhan, have been posted away, while our republican allies at court face exclusion. We must prepare for the worst: reassess the soldiers and farming households of the garrisons, restore grain shipments from upriver, and win over the academy students who will soon enter political life.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 整顿联合书院
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Reorganise the United Academies

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 襄阳的岳麓书院是湖广派官员、仪政士子的精神中心。但是它建立时起就奉行着忠于南朝的“爱国”教育。在南府频频发难的危急时刻，我们必须整顿人员，让岳麓教员们在我们的指挥下逐渐将把持朝政的倭吴丑类和朱明皇室区分开。以团结我内部思想以备不测。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Yuelu Academy in Xiangyang is the intellectual centre of Huguang’s officials and aspiring politicians. Its students study and debate public affairs before taking the examinations of the Assembly of Rites to enter Southern political life. Loyalty to the Southern realm has guided their education since the academy’s foundation. With the Southern Administration pressing us at every turn, its teachers must distinguish the Zheng rulers who dominate the government from the Zhu imperial house. Students won over in the lecture hall today may stand with us as provincial delegates tomorrow.

If the ministers who threaten us make their move, Xiangyang must have food and weapons.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 朱班博时代起，楚兵待遇优厚就远超南朝友军。其中更包括学自北朝的退伍年限和老兵集会。意图以此驱使受训听话的退伍士兵带领垦丁充实乡里，最终快速革新、改善久困于战火的湖广社会民生。时至今日，形成规模的“集会”老兵既熟悉营伍，也熟悉乡里。除了能在战时听令动员民众之外，我们也可以借助集会的力量对民众进行经济、生活上的动员准备。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Under Zhu Banbo, Chu soldiers enjoyed better conditions than their Southern allies. He also borrowed northern practices of fixed service terms and veterans’ assemblies, sending trained former soldiers to lead farming settlers and rebuild communities exhausted by war. These assemblies are now well established. Their veterans know both the army and the countryside; calling them together to organise food, relief and supplies will give wartime mobilisation a firm local foundation.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 在新政完全实现已不可阻挡的今天，局势已经逐渐脱离了杭州南府的掌控——这是好的！由此，我们需要重新平衡杭州的势力与西府各省。就像过去的“大礼议”改变了北明中期的国家格局，我们应当在各省代表共同支持的如今，从速召开额外的大礼议会（南明国家议会）和内阁会议。重新议定任官、赋额、军费、省制。以北朝、西夷、东洲施行的宪法/礼法制度为参照，重整政治。或可使朱姓天子终于挣脱桎梏，主持南朝国政。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Reform has carried the Southern realm beyond the old order of military fiefs. Hangzhou can no longer decide its government alone. Provincial delegates will debate appointments, taxation, military funding and provincial powers in the Assembly of Rites, while the cabinet and Six Ministries must govern under the revised constitution. We should first seek support from the Western provinces and overseas states, allowing the Zhu sovereign to govern constitutionally, free of the Southern Administration’s domination.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 随着各省学政（南明国会议员）在大礼议上以绝对多数表明了对新法的支持。以中央政府为核心的任官、田赋与军费改革终于统合为广泛承认的系列条陈，写入南明的国家“礼法”。依照新法，明廷，或者说现政权的明廷，终于结束了自西历15世纪初塞王之乱以来的地方割据的状态。\n\n当然，在行政上的统一于陈东阳重设行省布政司时就完成了。但那时的政策并未命令废止“封君”制度，也没有确定中央政府和地方的权力边界。只是南、西两府面临北朝南下的危机空前团结，以至于无人对南京（实际是杭州）统一执行军政事权、任免官员、捕杀不从的力量发出异议。即使有，也早在两府大兵的铁蹄铁铳下碾为尘埃——如今，这一切的努力终于刻入石头，万世难改。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites have supported the new provisions on appointments, land taxation and military funding, incorporating them into Southern Ming’s constitution. The Zhu succession endures, and the powers of the centre and provinces now rest on an accepted legal foundation.\n\nChen Dongyang’s restoration of provincial administrative commissions enabled common civil and military administration without fully resolving the status of former feudal lords and their local powers. Facing the northern advance, the Southern and Western Administrations had joined their armies to suppress resistance. Disputes then postponed by war have at last received a constitutional settlement.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 倭吴叛明称制的消息传来，江北大臣纷纷弹冠相庆。更有人提起牧家天子当年御辇南下的盛举。毕竟伪吴郑狗与西府各省决裂互斗中无暇北顾。南征统一或可一举成功。\n\n有心人的策动下，边将请拨军饷，并派员联络湖广的“有识之士”。然而，我朝却不是什么太平兴国之世界。国内正在推进的地权改革仍在继续。如果在改革期间卷入南朝的混战，未来是福是祸仍未可知也。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: News that the despised Wu have cast off Ming and claimed the throne has brought celebration among ministers north of the river. Some recall the Mu sovereign’s great southern expedition. If the pretenders are consumed by fighting the Western provinces, a new campaign might reunify the realm in a single stroke.\n\nFrontier commanders have requested funds and contacted “men of understanding” in Huguang. Yet our own realm is far from settled. Domestic government still requires troops and money; unfinished land reform would make a southern expedition more burdensome still. What could the empire gain by entering this struggle now?

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: With the fighting ended, local civil and military authority is passing under Wu rule. We may judge opponents individually and retain experienced local officials, or use victory to purge the old parties and make the army the foundation of the new order. D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
西元1678年春，时为北明吴国公的大明南京留守使、南京礼部尚书的（吴武宗）郑昭在他在海内外的一系列军事胜利后，单方面向朝廷上书，准备进京觐见大明天子。当是时，在三十年前的大宪战争中大获全胜的天津燕主及其国势还如烈火烹油。堪称北明战国末期的天下之雄。但郑氏的执拗战胜了朝臣的规劝和敌人的威胁。终于在同年六月成行。

这次觐见是一场北明从藩镇时期到诸侯时期近三百年来都未有人见过的盛大巡游。虽然吴国主在燕、秦、齐等势力的胁迫下，最终只带了5000卫士和一些官员随行。但在这队伍中包罗了吴国海陆军事力量在那个时代的全部精锐，南洋的海兵、倭国的刀牌手、女真掷弹兵的早期营队，甚至还包括一个由“极东殷人”流亡贵族组成的，向中国皇帝伸冤借兵的队伍。并携带着吴人在这个地球上纵横百年来所获得无数珍宝，以及又用了近万名民夫运送的安南、高棉贡米。与之相对的，则是在藩镇节度使制度下被小规模械斗和转运使卡要下，四时常乱，在饥荒边缘长久徘徊的中原。

在郑昭的觐见使团归来后。他当即改其称号为”至尊“，吴国随即见证了一个南北流民向自己及殖民地不断涌入的快速发展时期。而在那之后，郑昭及其继承者也开始以更加严苛的力度推进集权主义的“专权变法”及土地商品化改革。并最终稳固了我们作为南朝尊主，总领万国的基业。吴人前进的脚步从未停下，直至今天......
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng family has demanded a new dynasty and recognition from the provinces and overseas states. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power gives force to its claim, but the centuries-old Zhu succession still commands loyalty. The dispute unresolved in the Assembly of Rites and cabinet has now reached the provinces.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must answer. Recognition accepts Zheng government under the new constitution; taking up arms for Ming requires allies and preparations against Hangzhou’s forces. Others would use the crisis to leave the existing hierarchy and govern independently.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
Chen Dongyang entered Southern Ming as an exile from the Western Qin revolution. His alliance with Prince Zheng Qin brought the national republicans into the centre of southern government. Much of the army, revenue administration and overseas trading network remained under the Southern Command; the Cabinet depended on those institutions to carry out its appointments and land measures.

Every journey now requires another arrangement of ships, attendants and local escorts. The Cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to fund a guard answerable to the Chief Minister. Its pay and authority are before the court today.

$nesnd_chen.finance_rules$
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
Chen Dongyang came to Southern Ming as an exile from Western Qin and joined King Zheng Qin of Wu in reforming the state. Guoren republicans thereby entered the heart of Southern government. Reform now threatens the estates and titles of gentry, former feudal lords and officers; hostile verses and threatening letters continue to arrive. Master Dongguan remains absorbed in public affairs, but the cabinet cannot entrust his safety entirely to old alliances.

The court may fund a personal guard, keep him at his residence, or investigate his attendants and contacts. Protecting the leader of reform will cost money and place more power in the hands of the cabinet directing his guards.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Does the southern realm belong to the Zhu emperors, or to the Zheng rulers whose fleets and armies have carried it across the seas? Edicts travel from Nanjing to the same countries reached by Hangzhou’s merchants, tax collectors and warships. Centuries of Ming legitimacy now stand against the achievements and resources of Wu.\n\nXiangfan remains loyal to the Ming. Sichuan debates the reforms of the Southern Court, while overseas governors and Japanese lords consider the money, land and troops a new dynasty might demand. Their answers will soon have to be sustained by their own forces.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Whose realm is Southern Ming: the Zhu emperor’s, or the Zheng family’s creation? Nanjing retains the imperial succession, while the Southern Administration in Hangzhou commands the troops and revenues that sustain reform. The Western provinces and Hangzhou could postpone their dispute over sovereign and minister while resisting the North. With reform reaching deep into provincial life, they can no longer avoid the question of who will govern.\n\nHuguang’s academies and Xiangfan’s troops uphold the Zhu succession, while Sichuan’s republicans continue to debate the Southern Administration’s reforms. Governors in the Southern Seas and lords in Japan weigh the land, money and soldiers a new dynasty might demand. Representatives in the Assembly of Rites, ministers in the cabinet and provincial commanders will eventually have to answer for their choices.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The cabinet has delivered its proposed accord to [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. The Zhu emperor would continue to preside over the common court, while the provincial governments retain their territories and existing legal systems. D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The cabinet’s envoy has arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to seek our support for a settlement preserving the Ming dynasty. A constitution will define the powers of the centre and provinces. The Zhu sovereign will remain at the head of government, the cabinet and Six Ministries will administer under law, and provincial delegates will participate through the Assembly of Rites.\n\nAcceptance commits our government to the Zhu succession and this settlement. We retain our government, territory and existing laws. The status and commerce of overseas states will continue to be governed by their separate treaties.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Zheng envoy proposes to bring the mainland polities under direct provincial rule. Their Chinese territories covered by the agreement would pass to the central government, together with responsibility for their people, estates and workshops. The envoy has set out the lands to be transferred and now awaits our consent.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Southern Administration’s envoy offers clear terms: recognise Zheng accession and place our Chinese territories under direct central administration as provinces. Their separate military and political authority will end; appointments, taxation and military funding will fall under the new dynasty’s constitution and the cabinet and Six Ministries.\n\nThis would complete the centralising reforms long pursued by Hangzhou. Accepting means deciding who will govern and tax these lands. If our country also holds territory overseas, its government and boundaries there will be retained.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The southern mission has presented a new arrangement for the eastern seas. It asks the Japanese governments to recognize the Wu order and cede their own territories in Shikoku and Kyushu to direct Wu administration, retaining their other lands. The envoy awaits a reply while the ports and military offices verify the affected districts.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Southern Administration asks us to recognise the Zheng succession and surrender any territory we hold in Shikoku and Kyushu to direct Wu rule. Our government would retain its remaining lands.\n\nThe proposal ties a Southern dynastic succession to Japan’s borders. Acceptance would secure our place in the new order, at the cost of those territories. The court and the great houses must weigh that price before answering Hangzhou.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Zheng envoy has reached [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] seeking recognition for the new dynasty. Our government, territory and subject arrangements would remain in place. Port administration, trade and military expenses would be settled by separate agreements; the court seeks our political allegiance today.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Southern Administration asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to recognise the Zheng succession while retaining our government, territory and existing status. The Assembly of Rites and cabinet will settle the Southern constitution’s distribution of sovereign and provincial powers. Our commerce, ports and military obligations will remain matters for separate treaties.\n\nThe Zheng family needs recognition at home and overseas. Before answering, we must consider the place this succession would leave for our country.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: For a year, the provinces and states supporting Ming have upheld their commitment to reform. The provisions debated by provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites on appointments, land taxes and military funding now have a basis for enactment. The cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] to proclaim a constitution defining the powers of the centre and provinces.\n\nSince Chen Dongyang restored provincial administrative commissions, the Southern government has coordinated civil and military affairs, but the titles of former feudal lords still sustain local influence. Disputes set aside during resistance to the North can at last be settled in the assembly. The Zhu succession will endure, with sovereign, cabinet and provinces each exercising authority under the constitution.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The mainland provinces have consented to reorganization, and the overseas and Japanese governments have delivered their replies. D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The parties supporting Zheng have sustained their commitment to reform for a year. States due for provincial integration have accepted the transfer of their Chinese territories, and the Japanese governments have accepted the terms concerning Shikoku and Kyushu. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power now has a basis for establishing the new order.\n\nThe Assembly of Rites and cabinet will incorporate appointments, taxation, military funding and provincial government into a new constitution defining the powers of monarch and assembly. If the Zheng family accepts the throne, it must also accept these obligations. The Southern Administration, long governing in Ming’s name, will face the world under its own dynasty.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has proclaimed the revised constitution. Provincial delegates participate in the Assembly of Rites; the cabinet and Six Ministries conduct central government; provincial administrative commissions administer local affairs under the settlement. The Zhu house has gained room to govern beyond Hangzhou’s domination, while accepting constitutional limits on the sovereign.\n\nThe settlement preserves Southern Ming’s Confucian form of constitutional democracy and federation. Its provinces and overseas states retain their governments and territories, and the centre assumes the expense of maintaining the new institutions. Powers once contested by the Southern and Western Administrations through military strength now have an agreed constitutional basis.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has taken the throne and proclaimed the Wu constitution. Overseas states retaining their territories continue to govern themselves and deal with the new dynasty under their existing treaties.\n\nThe constitution recognises both the deliberative powers of the Assembly of Rites and the sovereign authority of the Zheng monarch, with the cabinet and Six Ministries conducting government accordingly. Generations of military power, commerce and overseas expansion since Zheng Zhao have at last become an empire ruled in the Zheng family’s own name.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: For centuries, relations between the court and the provincial governments have involved tribute, military obligations and dynastic authority. Zheng administration added overseas trade and a standing army to this imperial network. With the governments now choosing their accords, the central administration must provide the officials and funds promised in those agreements.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Chen Dongyang’s reforms have carried the Southern provinces beyond the military fiefs of the old Northern Ming order. Yet a deliberation in the assembly cannot by itself dissolve the grievances between the Southern and Western Administrations. With the parties supporting the same settlement, the centre must meet the agreed administrative expenses and put its proposed distribution of powers into practice.\n\nOverseas states also await fulfilment of the court’s commitments. Sustaining these arrangements month by month may bring the succession dispute back within reach of negotiation.

Neither side will have fulfilled its programme of reform, but the realm need no longer wait for a constitution that remains beyond agreement.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 南明易帜的消息传到了东洲。商馆将南洋的船期和各藩的动静抄在同一份报告上；当年独立战争留下的名字，又一次出现在议员们的案头。若南方诸国各自立政，郑氏的海上帝国便要分出新的关口与航路。共和国的国库、工厂和船队，也须各自交出一份账目。

The Zheng maritime empire that we fought for independence is again divided over who should rule it. Its opponents may seek support from our republic, while merchants watch for changes to the ports and routes on which they depend.\n\nWe can pursue those openings, but assistance abroad will draw on our own treasury and industry. The government must decide which relationships serve the republic and which commitments it can sustain.

We should decide whether to cultivate Sichuan, support the anti-Wu coalition, or keep our resources at home.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Ming Gives Way to Wu
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Ming–Wu Succession: Zheng Zhao’s Audience

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
In spring 1678, Zheng Zhao - Duke of Wu in Northern Ming, Nanjing regent and minister of rites - after a chain of military victories at home and abroad, petitioned the court to enter the capital and pay homage to the Ming Son of Heaven. At that time, the Tianjin Prince of Yan, victor of the great constitutional war thirty years earlier, still blazed in power. Yet Zheng's stubbornness overcame counsel and threats alike, and the journey took place that June.

This audience became a grand procession unseen for nearly three centuries, from warlord age to feudal-prince age in Northern Ming. Though coerced by Yan, Qin, and Qi powers into bringing only 5,000 guards and officials, Zheng's train contained elite land-sea forces of Wu's era: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese shield-swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadier units, even an exiled noble group of 'Far Eastern Yin people' seeking troops from the Chinese emperor. It carried treasures won by Wu over a century of global campaigns, plus Annamese and Khmer tribute rice borne by nearly ten thousand laborers. In stark contrast stood the famine-struck Central Plains under transport extortion and local armed strife.

After returning, Zheng Zhao at once took the title 'Supreme One.' Wu then entered rapid growth as refugees from north and south poured into its core and colonies. Zheng and his successors pushed harsh centralizing 'autocratic reform' and land commodification, ultimately securing our foundation as Southern Court overlord directing all nations. Wu's march has never ceased - to this very day...
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

Though virtue might decline, the mandate seemed unchanged. Yet today I have seen him: the Zhu boy is mortal too.\n—Zheng Zhao

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: After the Chief Minister’s Death

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
Chen Dongyang (courtesy name Manyue, 1772-[Date.GetString|v]) was a leading civic republican thinker and founding hero of the short-lived Western Qin revolutionary republic. Exiled from his own state, he worked with southern progressives and became chief architect of Southern Ming modernization as chief minister.

Yet reform brought fierce political upheaval and resistance from local power holders. As reform reached completion, Zheng Qin and allies came to fear republican ideals beyond their control. On [Date.GetString|v], while Chen departed for lecture tours in the Far East Continent, an unidentified Wa ronin shot him dead on deck with a short firearm.

After Chen's death, southern republicans who followed him immediately fell into accusation and factional dispute. Deng Mingyu, minister of revenue and fellow 'Four Gentlemen of the Republic,' moved toward Zheng Qin and the Southern Office. Zheng Diaojin, former administrator of Huguang, led part of the faction west to Sichuan under Xiao Huli.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Chen Dongyang is dead. Southern republicans have lost the leader of their reforms, while the cabinet and Six Ministries must redistribute his responsibilities. Provincial delegates still debate reform’s future in the Assembly of Rites, but Hangzhou is already courting the officials left without their leader.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Zhu of Ming, or Zheng of Wu? For politically active citizens of the Southern Court, this is a question asked every minute. From lecture platforms in Sichuan border schools to debate halls in Nanjing's ministry of rites, arguments, memorials, essays, and reports cry out everywhere. Yet there are more questions than answers, and more contention than deliberation.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Ming’s Zhu dynasty, or Wu’s Zheng house? For those able to take part in Southern Chinese politics, the question demands an answer at every moment. From village lecture halls on Sichuan’s frontier to the chamber of the Ministry of Rites in Nanjing, arguments, memorials, essays and reports call out to the public. There are more questions than answers, more quarrels than considered debate.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: About two centuries ago, the Toyotomi shogunate pacified Japan's Warring States with support from Wu's Prince of Ming, and later jointly defeated Korean forces backed by Yanjing Ming court and old Qi feudatory interests in struggles over Korea.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng foothold in Kyushu forms part of Wu’s maritime power and has long affected the interests of Japan’s great houses. With civil war threatening the Southern realm, rival envoys cross the sea seeking ships and supplies. The government has an opportunity to recover the Wu-held lands of Kyushu and reshape relations across the strait.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Zhu Banbo dead in battle, Chen Dongyang assassinated, Deng Mingyu defected, Zheng Diaojin fled west. Even mighty Mu Zhongtang, constrained by northern strife, cannot look south. In the Jinling palace no one remains who can face the Zheng-Wu Supreme directly. By China's millennia of history, dynastic transfer was only a matter of time - yet conservatives and reformers alike believed our age had transcended history. Dreams, however, seldom survive reality.\n\nAt that moment, by coincidence of Wu ruler's birthday, all Nanjing officials went to Hangzhou to offer congratulations, regardless of origin. In the Ming Gongzong court at Nanjing, only Zhu Jiangchen, son of old marshal Zhu Banbo and vice minister of war, remained. Three days later, Wu chancellor Hao Tingjiang and ten Wu ministers entered Jinling palace. Next day Gongzong enacted Yao-Shun style abdication in favor of Wu. Zheng Ju took the throne as emperor, proclaimed Great Wu, granted amnesty, and changed era to Tianyan, remembered as Emperor Tianyan and Wu Taizong. Ming Gongzong Zhu Kuobin was reduced to Ming feudatory prince and moved to Chongming Island in Fujian. A month later he was charged for excessive drinking at banquets; terrified, he hired a civilian vessel and fled eastward.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng family has demanded a new dynasty and recognition from the provinces and overseas states. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power gives force to its claim, but the centuries-old Zhu succession still commands loyalty. The dispute unresolved in the Assembly of Rites and cabinet has now reached the provinces.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must answer. Recognition accepts Zheng government under the new constitution; taking up arms for Ming requires allies and preparations against Hangzhou’s forces. Others would use the crisis to leave the existing hierarchy and govern independently.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Second Jingnan War

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
The Southern Ming turmoil that began with Wu-Ming dynastic transfer reached an unprecedented peak on [Date.GetString|v].

Former Ming loyalists, landlords sacrificed in land reform, and remnants of the early-century civic revolution - three groups with very different aims - united under pressure from the Zheng house of Southern Office. Zhu Jiangchen and Feng Yunshan of Chu, Wei Jian and Xiao Huli of Shu, Zhu Jingyin and Yang Xiuqing of Huai raised arms under the banner 'Overthrow Wu, restore Ming, pacify national calamity by Heaven's mandate.' Emperor Tianyan sent Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang, Lin Zexu, and Wu (Ii) Naosuke to suppress them.

When Tianyan took the throne, Southern Ming was nominally the world's leading empire. This upheaval shocked the world at once; from Far East Continent to distant England, states sent envoys. Today those envoys will witness a fierce eastern conflagration rekindled less than half a century after peace.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Proclamations against the succession have spread. Wu is assembling the central army to enforce recognition of Zheng rule; Ming loyalist provinces are gathering troops and supplies for common resistance. The Southern and Western Administrations, once united against the North, now face one another in arms.\n\nMaritime and river trade routes will carry armies and suffer the disruption of war. Overseas dependencies, neighbouring states and distant merchants must choose their course anew. Whoever wins will inherit the demands of those who shed blood for victory.

Rather than full explosion of contradictions, decisive Southern Court politicians delayed imperial collapse through firm choices. Even amid Wu-Ming dynastic upheaval, regional governors chose no effective resistance and accepted Wu narratives of total corruption by the Ming emperor and his magnates, preserving a fragile peace in South China.

In one sense, this implies the sun-and-moon dynasty had long become rotten wood no one wished to die with. Zhu Kuobin, the last emperor to defend court order, may simply have been born at the wrong time.

Yet this survivor of four centuries of warlord politics lost much. The age of war-peace confrontation ended, but opponents, regional prejudice among old feudatory populations, and new radical groups still move in the shadows of the new era, cloaking the nation's road forward in dense fog.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Local opposition has failed to form a coalition for common war. Provinces and overseas states that remain loyal recognise Zheng rule, while others have left the previous hierarchy. Hangzhou can continue governing the centre, but cannot treat every silence as consent.\n\nThe new dynasty must appoint officials and govern under its constitution, while sustaining authority with the troops and revenues it possesses. Unresolved relations with the provinces and states will be shaped by future development, negotiation and conflict.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The internal chaos raised by Zheng traitors has finally ended in the victory of those on the righteous path. This is not an age to praise. Loyalists killed loyalists; republicans attacked republicans. Zheng's group was not originally the most rotten faction of old Ming, yet their thirst for power and singular status in the old state pushed all of us into the abyss of war. As victors, we must ensure this never repeats.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The coalition has defeated Wu’s central army. The Ming cause brought the Western provinces and their allies together; victory now raises another question: who will govern from Nanjing?\n\nThe Zhu house still claims the throne, while victorious provincial leaders are reluctant to surrender their military and political authority. Republicans want the citizens who fought together to share in a new deliberative government. Whether the wartime coalition can accommodate these demands will determine the Southern realm’s future constitution.

If civil war erupts in Ming (Wu), Japan - the largest outer feudatory of the Ming court - must quickly prepare to defend our interests and perhaps the order of Shenzhou itself.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Southern civil war has brought Kyushu back to the centre of Japanese politics. Zheng ports, trade routes and garrisons on the island support Wu’s maritime power and affect the interests of Japanese lords and merchants.\n\nBoth Wu and its opponents seek Japanese intervention, offering to return the Zheng-held parts of Kyushu after victory. The side we support will determine our allies across the sea and the government from which we must claim our reward.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: When Zhu Banbo reorganised Huguang, he repaired the fortifications of Xiangyang, brought young officers into teaching, and exchanged military ironware for grain from Sichuan. Wounded and retired soldiers entered supply services and farming garrisons. Republicans who remained in Xiangyang helped the governor-general reform Yuelu Academy. Over twenty years, the army, land revenues and academies became closely bound to his government, with Chen Dongyang supporting it at court. Xiangyang’s troops came to be regarded as the leaders of the New Western Administration, an indispensable pillar of the Southern Ming federation.\n\nThe Zheng family once supported Zhu Banbo vigorously. Now it repeatedly accuses Xiangyang of withholding taxes and concealing households. Southern officers friendly to Huguang, including Shi Yuanfu and Lin Hanhan, have been posted away, while our republican allies at court face exclusion. We must prepare for the worst: reassess the soldiers and farming households of the garrisons, restore grain shipments from upriver, and win over the academy students who will soon enter political life.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Reorganise the United Academies

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 襄阳书院曾为湖广造就军官、教员与办事之吏。恢复各县选送生员的办法，使总督府的政令有人施行，地方的粮饷有人核算。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Yuelu Academy in Xiangyang is the intellectual centre of Huguang’s officials and aspiring politicians. Its students study and debate public affairs before taking the examinations of the Assembly of Rites to enter Southern political life. Loyalty to the Southern realm has guided their education since the academy’s foundation. With the Southern Administration pressing us at every turn, its teachers must distinguish the Zheng rulers who dominate the government from the Zhu imperial house. Students won over in the lecture hall today may stand with us as provincial delegates tomorrow.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Huguang’s workshops and Sichuan’s grain boats sustained Xiangyang when we fought the Mu forces. If the ministers who threaten us make their move, Xiangyang must have food and weapons.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Under Zhu Banbo, Chu soldiers enjoyed better conditions than their Southern allies. These assemblies are now well established. Their veterans know both the army and the countryside; calling them together to organise food, relief and supplies will give wartime mobilisation a firm local foundation.

We should first seek support from the Western provinces and overseas states, allowing the Zhu sovereign to govern constitutionally, free of the Southern Administration’s domination.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 南京终于收到各府签押的新约。任官、田赋与军费的争议，被列入朝廷与各府共同遵守的章程。朱姓王室保有帝统，吴府仍经营其广阔的海陆产业，地方总督也得以凭明文约定参与国政。\n\n这些约定经历了反复交涉。每一笔赋额、每一个官缺，都牵动着一支军队或一群士人的生计。如今，[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]得以沿用旧有的名号，开始组织一套新的政治生活。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites have supported the new provisions on appointments, land taxation and military funding, incorporating them into Southern Ming’s constitution. The Zhu succession endures, and the powers of the centre and provinces now rest on an accepted legal foundation.\n\nChen Dongyang’s restoration of provincial administrative commissions enabled common civil and military administration without fully resolving the status of former feudal lords and their local powers. Facing the northern advance, the Southern and Western Administrations had joined their armies to suppress resistance. Disputes then postponed by war have at last received a constitutional settlement.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: News that the despised Wu have cast off Ming and claimed the throne has brought celebration among ministers north of the river. Some recall the Mu sovereign’s great southern expedition. If the pretenders are consumed by fighting the Western provinces, a new campaign might reunify the realm in a single stroke.\n\nFrontier commanders have requested funds and contacted “men of understanding” in Huguang. Yet our own realm is far from settled. Domestic government still requires troops and money; unfinished land reform would make a southern expedition more burdensome still. What could the empire gain by entering this struggle now?

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 战事平定以后，地方的田赋、官缺与营伍陆续归入[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]的统辖。吴府经营已久的中央机关开始接收各省文书，商人催问战时借款，各营则呈报军功与封赏。\n\n新朝拥有熟悉财赋和海贸的官员，也拥有足以执行命令的军队。如何任用旧官、处置抵抗者，并使地方重新生产和纳税，将决定这些力量能够建立怎样的统治。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: With the fighting ended, local civil and military authority is passing under Wu rule. The new dynasty must now govern: production and trade disrupted by war must recover, people need their livelihoods, and officials and scholars who opposed Zheng will not disappear with defeat.\n\nHangzhou’s accumulated military and fiscal strength can sustain reconstruction. We may judge opponents individually and retain experienced local officials, or use victory to purge the old parties and make the army the foundation of the new order. These decisions will show the realm what government in the Zheng family’s own name means.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 明朝朱姓，还是吴国郑氏？这对于中国南朝有能力参预政治的国人来说，是一个每分每秒都要自问的难题。从川边乡校的讲习台到南京礼部的议会殿。争论、札子、散文、报道，各式各样体裁的文字都在对人们呼喊。却是问多于答，争大于论。

西元1678年春，时为北明吴国公的大明南京留守使、南京礼部尚书的（吴武宗）郑昭在他在海内外的一系列军事胜利后，单方面向朝廷上书，准备进京觐见大明天子。当是时，在三十年前的大宪战争中大获全胜的天津燕主及其国势还如烈火烹油。堪称北明战国末期的天下之雄。但郑氏的执拗战胜了朝臣的规劝和敌人的威胁。终于在同年六月成行。

这次觐见是一场北明从藩镇时期到诸侯时期近三百年来都未有人见过的盛大巡游。虽然吴国主在燕、秦、齐等势力的胁迫下，最终只带了5000卫士和一些官员随行。但在这队伍中包罗了吴国海陆军事力量在那个时代的全部精锐，南洋的海兵、倭国的刀牌手、女真掷弹兵的早期营队，甚至还包括一个由“极东殷人”流亡贵族组成的，向中国皇帝伸冤借兵的队伍。并携带着吴人在这个地球上纵横百年来所获得无数珍宝，以及又用了近万名民夫运送的安南、高棉贡米。与之相对的，则是在藩镇节度使制度下被小规模械斗和转运使卡要下，四时常乱，在饥荒边缘长久徘徊的中原。

在郑昭的觐见使团归来后。他当即改其称号为”至尊“，吴国随即见证了一个南北流民向自己及殖民地不断涌入的快速发展时期。而在那之后，郑昭及其继承者也开始以更加严苛的力度推进集权主义的“专权变法”及土地商品化改革。并最终稳固了我们作为南朝尊主，总领万国的基业。吴人前进的脚步从未停下，直至今天......
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: 南京颁下禅位诏书，命各府奉郑氏正朔。吴府所辖的中央军、财赋机关与海外商馆已开始改用新朝名号，地方总督也须上表，承认郑氏统辖海内外的权力。\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]的军队、官员与地方议局，长期依照同明朝订立的旧约行事。承认易代，便须同吴朝重新确定这些权利；举兵奉明，则须联络各府，准备迎击南府的中央军。亦有人主张退出旧有的隶属，自行主持地方国政。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Zheng family has demanded a new dynasty and recognition from the provinces and overseas states. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power gives force to its claim, but the centuries-old Zhu succession still commands loyalty. The dispute unresolved in the Assembly of Rites and cabinet has now reached the provinces.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must answer. Recognition accepts Zheng government under the new constitution; taking up arms for Ming requires allies and preparations against Hangzhou’s forces. Others would use the crisis to leave the existing hierarchy and govern independently.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Proclamations against the succession have spread. The Southern and Western Administrations, once united against the North, now face one another in arms.\n\nMaritime and river trade routes will carry armies and suffer the disruption of war. Overseas dependencies, neighbouring states and distant merchants must choose their course anew. Whoever wins will inherit the demands of those who shed blood for victory.

Republicans want the citizens who fought together to share in a new deliberative government. Whether the wartime coalition can accommodate these demands will determine the Southern realm’s future constitution.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before:
Chen Dongyang entered Southern Ming as an exile from the Western Qin revolution. His alliance with Prince Zheng Qin brought the national republicans into the centre of southern government. Much of the army, revenue administration and overseas trading network remained under the Southern Command; the Cabinet depended on those institutions to carry out its appointments and land measures.

Every journey now requires another arrangement of ships, attendants and local escorts. The Cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to fund a guard answerable to the Chief Minister. Its pay and authority are before the court today.

$nesnd_chen.finance_rules$
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
Chen Dongyang came to Southern Ming as an exile from Western Qin and joined King Zheng Qin of Wu in reforming the state. Guoren republicans thereby entered the heart of Southern government. Reform now threatens the estates and titles of gentry, former feudal lords and officers; hostile verses and threatening letters continue to arrive. Master Dongguan remains absorbed in public affairs, but the cabinet cannot entrust his safety entirely to old alliances.

The court may fund a personal guard, keep him at his residence, or investigate his attendants and contacts. Protecting the leader of reform will cost money and place more power in the hands of the cabinet directing his guards.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Does the southern realm belong to the Zhu emperors, or to the Zheng rulers whose fleets and armies have carried it across the seas? Edicts travel from Nanjing to the same countries reached by Hangzhou’s merchants, tax collectors and warships. Centuries of Ming legitimacy now stand against the achievements and resources of Wu.\n\nXiangfan remains loyal to the Ming. Sichuan debates the reforms of the Southern Court, while overseas governors and Japanese lords consider the money, land and troops a new dynasty might demand. Their answers will soon have to be sustained by their own forces.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Whose realm is Southern Ming: the Zhu emperor’s, or the Zheng family’s creation? Nanjing retains the imperial succession, while the Southern Administration in Hangzhou commands the troops and revenues that sustain reform. The Western provinces and Hangzhou could postpone their dispute over sovereign and minister while resisting the North. With reform reaching deep into provincial life, they can no longer avoid the question of who will govern.\n\nHuguang’s academies and Xiangfan’s troops uphold the Zhu succession, while Sichuan’s republicans continue to debate the Southern Administration’s reforms. Governors in the Southern Seas and lords in Japan weigh the land, money and soldiers a new dynasty might demand. Representatives in the Assembly of Rites, ministers in the cabinet and provincial commanders will eventually have to answer for their choices.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Zheng envoy proposes to bring the mainland polities under direct provincial rule. D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Revising the Constitution

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The provincial governments have honored their agreements for a year. Local administrations conduct their own affairs within the common court, and the Zhu emperor can proclaim a renewed compact among the southern polities.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: For a year, the provinces and states supporting Ming have upheld their commitment to reform. The provisions debated by provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites on appointments, land taxes and military funding now have a basis for enactment. The cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] to proclaim a constitution defining the powers of the centre and provinces.\n\nSince Chen Dongyang restored provincial administrative commissions, the Southern government has coordinated civil and military affairs, but the titles of former feudal lords still sustain local influence. Disputes set aside during resistance to the North can at last be settled in the assembly. The Zhu succession will endure, with sovereign, cabinet and provinces each exercising authority under the constitution.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Proclaim the renewed compact.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Proclaim the constitution.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Foundations of Wu
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: A Constitution for the Succession

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The mainland provinces have consented to reorganization, and the overseas and Japanese governments have delivered their replies. A year of cooperation has sustained the administration, armed forces and sea routes. The Zheng court is ready to proclaim its dynasty and assume control of the agreed territories.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The parties supporting Zheng have sustained their commitment to reform for a year. States due for provincial integration have accepted the transfer of their Chinese territories, and the Japanese governments have accepted the terms concerning Shikoku and Kyushu. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power now has a basis for establishing the new order.\n\nThe Assembly of Rites and cabinet will incorporate appointments, taxation, military funding and provincial government into a new constitution defining the powers of monarch and assembly. If the Zheng family accepts the throne, it must also accept these obligations. The Southern Administration, long governing in Ming’s name, will face the world under its own dynasty.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Compact Proclaimed
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Constitution Established

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The proclamation has been issued, and the provincial signatures and seals have entered a common register. The Zhu emperor continues to preside over the southern court while local governments administer their own affairs. Its obligations will shape the finances, construction and diplomacy of the renewed order.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has proclaimed the revised constitution. Provincial delegates participate in the Assembly of Rites; the cabinet and Six Ministries conduct central government; provincial administrative commissions administer local affairs under the settlement. The Zhu house has gained room to govern beyond Hangzhou’s domination, while accepting constitutional limits on the sovereign.\n\nThe settlement preserves Southern Ming’s Confucian form of constitutional democracy and federation. Its provinces and overseas states retain their governments and territories, and the centre assumes the expense of maintaining the new institutions. Powers once contested by the Southern and Western Administrations through military strength now have an agreed constitutional basis.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Wu Dynasty
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The Wu Dynasty Established

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The new seals have reached the provinces that accepted integration. Treasuries and military offices exchange their registers; overseas governments issue letters recognizing the dynasty, and the ceded Japanese districts begin changing administrations. The Zheng house has converted its military, fiscal and maritime power into a new title, with obligations it must now fulfil.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has taken the throne and proclaimed the Wu constitution. The centre has assumed administration of the Chinese territories that accepted integration, together with the lands ceded in Shikoku and Kyushu. Overseas states retaining their territories continue to govern themselves and deal with the new dynasty under their existing treaties.\n\nThe constitution recognises both the deliberative powers of the Assembly of Rites and the sovereign authority of the Zheng monarch, with the cabinet and Six Ministries conducting government accordingly. Generations of military power, commerce and overseas expansion since Zheng Zhao have at last become an empire ruled in the Zheng family’s own name.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Reconciling the Realm

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: For centuries, relations between the court and the provincial governments have involved tribute, military obligations and dynastic authority. Zheng administration added overseas trade and a standing army to this imperial network. With the governments now choosing their accords, the central administration must provide the officials and funds promised in those agreements.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Chen Dongyang’s reforms have carried the Southern provinces beyond the military fiefs of the old Northern Ming order. Yet a deliberation in the assembly cannot by itself dissolve the grievances between the Southern and Western Administrations. With the parties supporting the same settlement, the centre must meet the agreed administrative expenses and put its proposed distribution of powers into practice.\n\nOverseas states also await fulfilment of the court’s commitments. Sustaining these arrangements month by month may bring the succession dispute back within reach of negotiation.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Two years of negotiations have produced no common settlement. Provincial governments continue to administer their territories, and the central accords have not secured a general agreement. The existing borders, governments and treaties remain in force.\n\nThe court may now end this round of negotiations and recognize the arrangements currently in place.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The succession dispute has lasted two years without a settlement acceptable to all parties. The Southern provinces and overseas states continue to exercise their existing powers, while the divide between Ming and Wu has not produced a common war.\n\nWe can close these constitutional negotiations and accept the present borders, governments and treaty relations. Neither side will have fulfilled its programme of reform, but the realm need no longer wait for a constitution that remains beyond agreement.
